title: Aristotle Meteorology I.9-I.12: source-only causal and contrast graph

provenance.cached_scope: Webster English translation, Parts 9-12, 2162 words; paraphrased here in full
provenance.contextual_note: The linked page is Thomas Aquinas, Sentencia super Meteora, with a Leonine 1886 text; it confirms a medieval exposition context, not a circa-1420 witness or a Voynich plaintext.

nodes.description: The sun's approach and retreat drive dissipation and condensation, hence generation and destruction.
Moisture surrounding the earth remains the material source.
Sunlight and heat from above evaporate the moisture.
The exhaled water rises; it retains the heat that lifted it.
Heat is lost by dispersal upward or quenching during ascent; cold place and lost heat cool the vapour.
Cooled vapour condenses and changes from air to water.
Once water has formed it descends to earth.
Air that condenses into water is called cloud.
Residue after cloud condenses into water; a barren-cloud sign of fair weather rather than rain.
Small falling drops are drizzle; larger drops are rain.

causal_cycle.qualification: The cycle follows the sun: vapour tends upward when the sun is near and water downward when it recedes, while the sequence itself remains ordered. Aristotle compares it to a circular river partly air and partly water.

nodes.description: Some daytime vapour does not rise high because the fire-to-water ratio is small; it cools and descends at night.
Vapour first condenses to water, with heat insufficient to dry it and climate or season warm enough to prevent freezing.
Vapour freezes before it has condensed back into water; it is associated with winter and colder places.
Clear sky permits raising; still air permits condensation. Both dew and hoar-frost require these conditions.
Vapour rises from hollow and watery places; a heavy burden limits its height.
Hoar-frost is absent on mountains in the account because high air motion dissolves the gathering and the vapour does not rise high.
Outside Pontus, south wind accompanies dew and north does not; south brings warmth, north cold that quenches evaporation.
In Pontus the south is too cool to cause enough evaporation, while north cold concentrates heat by recoil and yields more evaporation; wells likewise emit more vapour in north than south wind.
Water already formed on the earth's surface does not freeze in the same way as water in cloud-region conditions.

dew_frost_and_lower_conditions.contrast: Dew and frost share a low vapour path but split at the order of phase change: water first then no freeze versus freeze before water. Warmth makes dew more common; cold makes frost more common, but Pontus reverses the ordinary wind association.

nodes.description: Rain, snow and hail are three bodies condensed by cold in the upper region.
Rain and dew are treated as one kind in different amount: rain uses much vapour gathered over a larger region and longer time; dew is small and forms in a day over a small area.
Snow and hoar-frost are treated as one kind in different amount and cloud/vapour stage: cloud freezing yields snow, vapour freezing yields frost.
Hail has no corresponding lower vapour-region phenomenon, unlike the rain/dew and snow/frost pairs.
Hail is ice formed when already formed water freezes faster than it descends.
Large angular hail indicates short fall and freezing near the earth; distant fall abrades stones into smaller rounder forms.
Warm surrounding air concentrates cold within by recoil; the same reversal makes lower earth cold in warm weather and warm in frost.
In warm seasons, concentrated cold makes cloud become water suddenly, producing large drops and violent showers.
Hail is uncommon in dry summer, more common in moist spring and moisture-returning autumn; late summer is possible. It is commoner in warm places while snow is commoner in cold places.
Water warmed beforehand is said to freeze more quickly; the text gives sun-warmed water and Pontus fishermen pouring warm water around reeds on ice as examples.
Arabia and Ethiopia receive summer rather than winter rain, in torrents and repeatedly in one day, attributed to extreme heat and recoil cooling clouds.

rejected_or_negated_accounts.claim: Hail cannot be explained by cloud being pushed into a cold upper atmosphere and freezing there.
rejected_or_negated_accounts.attribution: unnamed proponents; explicitly opposed by Aristotle
reasons: hail is not found at great height though that theory predicts it
large angular stones and observed near-ground clouds imply short fall and near-ground freezing
snow, unlike hail, is the high-mountain comparison

rejected_or_negated_accounts.claim: Anaxagoras' explanation of violent showers is opposed.
rejected_or_negated_accounts.account_given: cloud descends into warm air; farther descent increases the effect

rejected_or_negated_accounts.claim: Hailstone growth by liquid droplets joining cannot explain hail.
reasons: solid bodies do not coalesce like liquids
the drops must already have been large while suspended

rejected_or_negated_accounts.claim: A cloud can freeze before becoming water.
rejected_or_negated_accounts.reason: the text says freezing requires formed water; suspension time and fall-time ordering are the issue

asymmetric_relations_for_future_text_rep.relation: rain:dew and snow:frost are paired correspondences, while hail has no lower counterpart
asymmetric_relations_for_future_text_rep.why_asymmetric: Two upper/lower mappings exist and the third explicitly fails to map.
asymmetric_relations_for_future_text_rep.observable_representation_needed: At least two repeated paired frames plus a third upper phenomenon with an explicit negative, absent-lower slot, or equivalent exception marker; simple recurrence or co-occurrence is insufficient.
asymmetric_relations_for_future_text_rep.multiword_constraint: Constrains four pair-role words and a hail-role word together without requiring any one word to be known first.

asymmetric_relations_for_future_text_rep.relation: vapour freezing before condensation yields frost; cloud freezing yields snow; formed water freezing before descent yields hail
asymmetric_relations_for_future_text_rep.why_asymmetric: The same broad material path branches according to the order of phase transitions and altitude.
asymmetric_relations_for_future_text_rep.observable_representation_needed: A directed multi-stage clause with distinct state nodes and ordered transition markers; an unordered list of weather terms cannot represent the contrast.
asymmetric_relations_for_future_text_rep.multiword_constraint: Constrains terms for vapour/cloud/water and three outcome terms jointly.

asymmetric_relations_for_future_text_rep.relation: rain exceeds dew in collected amount, spatial source and collection time; snow exceeds frost analogously
asymmetric_relations_for_future_text_rep.why_asymmetric: The paired names share causes but differ systematically in magnitude and extent.
asymmetric_relations_for_future_text_rep.observable_representation_needed: The same pair heads must recur with explicit quantity, duration or spatial modifiers that preserve the large/small ordering; isolated value-like tokens do not suffice.
asymmetric_relations_for_future_text_rep.multiword_constraint: Constrains both members of each pair and their amount/extent field.

asymmetric_relations_for_future_text_rep.relation: dew follows south rather than north wind generally, but north rather than south in Pontus
asymmetric_relations_for_future_text_rep.why_asymmetric: The same outcome and wind alternatives reverse under a named geographic condition.
asymmetric_relations_for_future_text_rep.observable_representation_needed: A location-conditioned contrast with two wind-direction slots and opposite polarity, plus an explicit exception boundary; frequency alone cannot encode it.
asymmetric_relations_for_future_text_rep.multiword_constraint: Constrains dew, two directional terms, and a location term as one relation.

asymmetric_relations_for_future_text_rep.relation: hail's near-ground formation is inferred from large angular stones and short fall; high-altitude freezing is rejected
asymmetric_relations_for_future_text_rep.why_asymmetric: Observed shape and violence support one formation location while the attributed rival predicts the opposite height.
asymmetric_relations_for_future_text_rep.observable_representation_needed: A written observation→inference chain containing shape/size, fall duration or height, and an explicit rejected alternative.
asymmetric_relations_for_future_text_rep.multiword_constraint: Constrains hail, shape/size descriptors, vertical-location terms and negation.

asymmetric_relations_for_future_text_rep.relation: clear calm permits dew/frost condensation; mist is a sign of fair weather rather than a rain cause
asymmetric_relations_for_future_text_rep.why_asymmetric: The same atmospheric material can be a prerequisite in one frame and merely an indicator in another.
asymmetric_relations_for_future_text_rep.observable_representation_needed: Conditional prerequisite syntax and a separate sign-versus-outcome relation, retaining explicit absence of wind.
asymmetric_relations_for_future_text_rep.multiword_constraint: Constrains dew/frost, mist, clear/calm conditions and rain as distinct roles.

source_ceiling.historical_transfer: The text can supply a finite conceptual comparison, but it does not establish that the Voynich manuscript encodes this system.
source_ceiling.language: No Latin substitution, transliteration or word assignment is made.
source_ceiling.semantic_status: No Voynich meaning, image object, sentence boundary or universal recipe/document rule is inferred.
